finding.claim: Authentication is not implemented in notes.py: g.user is read on lines 28, 35 and 44 but never assigned here. If the code that sets g.user derives it from client-controlled input (header, cookie, or query parameter) without verification, every note can be read, written or shared by any caller.
finding.source: g.user, set outside notes.py (not present in the audited code)
finding.sink: can_view (notes.py:8) and can_edit (notes.py:17), guarding read, write and share

trace.note: can_view checks owner == user or user in shared

finding.guards_checked: The authorization checks in this file (can_view, can_edit, require_view, require_edit) are correct for owner and shared-user cases. The authentication that sets g.user is absent from this file and could not be verified; exploitability is conditional on that external code.

verdict.guard_found: can_view (notes.py:8) and can_edit (notes.py:17) are bool-returning checks, and require_view/require_edit (notes.py:11-13, 20-22) abort(403) on failure. The trace's line references are accurate. The g.user value is never set anywhere in the directory: the only .py file is notes.py, and a grep for `g.user =`, `before_request`, or auth helpers finds nothing.
verdict.reason: Every trace line (notes.py:8, 11-13, 17, 20-22, 28, 35, 44) matches its description and the checks are correct, but whether anyone can forge g.user depends on code that sets it (absent from this directory), so exploitability cannot be decided here; as written in notes.py alone, an unset g.user raises AttributeError at notes.py:28/35/44 rather than granting access.

finding.claim: State-changing routes (PUT /n/<nid> and POST /n/<nid>/share) have no CSRF protection in this file. If authentication is cookie-based, a cross-site request can modify note bodies or add sharing targets as a logged-in victim.
finding.source: Cross-site request from a victim's browser carrying the victim's session cookie

trace.note: PUT route accepts write without a token check
POST share route accepts sharing without a token check

finding.guards_checked: No CSRF token, Origin or Referer check, or SameSite handling appears in this file. Exploitability depends on the external authentication mechanism (cookie-based or not) and framework settings, which were not audited.

verdict.guard_found: No explicit CSRF guard in notes.py. The effective block is incidental: the sinks read `request.json["body"]` (notes.py:37) and `request.json["user"]` (notes.py:45), and Flask/Werkzeug's `request.json` rejects non-JSON content types. A cross-site HTML form cannot send `application/json`, and it cannot send PUT at all. A cross-site fetch with a JSON body needs a CORS preflight, and this app sends no CORS headers. The ownership checks in can_edit/require_edit (notes.py:16-22, 35, 44) are authorization, not CSRF protection.
verdict.reason: The trace lines match the code, but the cross-site vectors are blocked: a form cannot send PUT (notes.py:32), and the JSON body that notes.py:37 and notes.py:45 require cannot come from a simple cross-site form, so only a same-origin or CORS-permitted request can reach the sinks. This depends on the Flask/Werkzeug version enforcing JSON content types, which is not pinned in the code available here, so the claim is refuted for the standard browser vectors but not proven impossible.

finding.claim: Sharing cannot be revoked. The shared list only grows and no route removes entries, so an owner cannot withdraw access granted by mistake or to a user who should no longer have it.

trace.note: append is the only mutation of shared

finding.guards_checked: Only the owner can share (require_edit, notes.py:44). This is a missing capability rather than an authorization bypass.

verdict.guard_found: require_edit (notes.py:20-22, called at notes.py:44) limits sharing to the owner. This does not block the claimed effect; it only shows that the owner is the sole actor who can change sharing.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: share() at notes.py:41-46 only appends to note["shared"] at line 45, and nothing else in notes.py removes entries. But the only party affected by the missing revocation is the owner, who already controls the note, and the claim describes a missing feature, not an attacker reaching a power they lack, so it is not a security vulnerability (notes.py:44-45).

finding.claim: Unknown note IDs raise KeyError (HTTP 500) while existing notes the caller cannot access return 403, so an authenticated caller can determine whether a note ID exists.

trace.note: read() indexes NOTES[nid] with no default

finding.guards_checked: The lookup is a plain dict access, so there is no path traversal or injection. Impact depends on whether note IDs are guessable, which is generated outside this file.

verdict.guard_found: none. notes.py:27, 34 and 43 index NOTES[nid] with no default and no try/except, and no errorhandler for KeyError is defined in notes.py. The only guards are require_view/can_view (notes.py:12-13) and can_edit/require_edit (notes.py:17-22), and these run only after the lookup succeeds, so they never run for an unknown ID.
verdict.reason: For an unknown nid, NOTES[nid] at notes.py:27 raises KeyError before require_view at notes.py:28 runs, so Flask returns a 500; for an existing note the caller without access hits abort(403) at notes.py:13, so the two responses differ and reveal whether an ID exists. Impact depends on how unguessable the IDs are, which this file does not show, and g.user is set outside this file as well, so the authenticated-caller precondition is taken from the candidate rather than verified here.

finding.claim: The share endpoint accepts any JSON type as the target user, performs no existence check and no de-duplication, and imposes no size cap, so an owner can grow a note's shared list without limit and store non-string values.

trace.note: require_edit limits callers to the owner
unvalidated value appended to shared list

finding.guards_checked: Owner-only access (require_edit) limits impact to the owner's own notes. No type, existence, duplicate or size checks exist.

verdict.guard_found: require_edit (notes.py:20-22) aborts with 403 when can_edit fails, and it is called as a bare statement at notes.py:44. Because abort() raises, that call is effective and only the note owner reaches line 45. Nothing else checks the type, existence, duplicates, or size of the appended value.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (notes.py:41, 44, 45), but only the note's owner can reach the append at notes.py:45 via require_edit (notes.py:20-22), and the owner already has full power to share the note with any user. Growing the owner's own shared list or storing odd JSON values only affects that owner's note, and membership checks in can_view (notes.py:8) still work on non-string values, so this is input-validation hygiene rather than a security vulnerability.
